highlight.text: We may call his Don Quixote in the Berlin Gallery sketchy, if we choose to compare it with a Meissonier. But we may as justly call it fresco-like, if we compare it from a greater distance. It is not, in truth, the picture, but the eye of the spectator which is sketchy.

source.label: Sadleir: “Daumier’s love for Quixote was part of his romantic birthright”

work.text: Most clearly is this sympathy expressed in the long series of his Quixote pictures. … Cervantes’ hero, at once moving and laughable, dignified and absurd, appealed not only to the artist’s keen sense of the ridiculous but also to his feeling for sombre simplicity and to his pity for futility.

source.author: Michael Sadleir
source.title: Daumier: The Man and the Artist

moment.text: In his numerous renderings of Don Quixote, he has made symbols of the two figures, that give an almost metaphysical value to the conceptions of " fat " and " thin."

source.author: Julius Meier-Graefe
source.title: Modern Art: Being a Contribution to a New System of Aesthetics, vol. 1

matters.text: He experienced failing eyesight and poverty there, although he continued to produce lithographs and paint, often on the theme of Don Quixote.
One need not force the argument further or insist that the artist saw in Quixote one who, like himself, had pursued vainly every dream.

source.author: Michael Sadleir
source.title: Daumier: The Man and the Artist
